unit.title: SwiftUI bootcamp: first app and data flow
unit.summary: Seven dedicated beginner lessons establish an app, controls, composition, fixtures, ownership and collection editing.

lessons.title: Create your first SwiftUI iOS app
lessons.summary: Build the smallest complete app, choose the right target and simulator, and explain the scene-to-view path before adding features.
objectives: Create an iOS SwiftUI scratch target and identify its executable entry.
Distinguish a target, scheme, SDK, deployment minimum and simulator destination.
Read the App, Scene and View description path.
Record compiler and simulator launch evidence separately.

sections.title: A first screen establishes the platform boundary
sections.html:
You already know how an Android Activity starts and renders a Compose screen. On iOS, begin with a similarly small executable, but learn the names of its boundaries before translating architecture. Xcode is the development application. An Xcode project organizes targets, resources and settings; a target describes one product to build; a scheme chooses actions such as Build, Run and Test and their configuration. A simulator destination is the device and operating-system runtime used for that action. These are related choices, not different names for a Gradle variant.

This lesson builds a greeting with synthetic data. It requires a Mac with an installed Xcode that includes the iOS SDK, an installed iOS simulator runtime, and a scratch iOS App target. Use a minimum deployment target of iOS 17 for the whole beginner track. Xcode 15 or later supplies the Swift 5.9-era features used later. A newer installed compiler is fine; that statement is a course baseline, not a claim about the newest recommended Xcode. Session 070 supplies the language practice; no earlier iOS project is assumed.

A successful compiler result, a running simulator app, and a working preview are separate observations. Record each when you actually perform it. This course supplies source and acceptance expectations; it has not executed your new app. Keep the company checkout as reading material and create the scratch project outside its app targets.

sections.title: Create the project and find the product settings
sections.html:
Open Xcode and choose File → New → Project. Select the iOS App template. Use a product name such as FirstSteps, SwiftUI for the interface and Swift for the language. Template wording can vary by Xcode version. Choose no persistence integration for this initial project, and include a unit-test target if offered; it can also be added later. An organization identifier such as example.learning contributes to the bundle identifier, which identifies the app product rather than the Swift module you import.

Save to a learner-owned directory. In the project navigator, select the project and then the app target. Find its minimum deployment setting and set iOS 17. The deployment target means the oldest supported runtime; the installed SDK means which API declarations the compiler can see. Selecting an iOS 17 simulator does not independently change that target setting. Swift language mode is another setting; it controls language rules and diagnostics rather than deciding the simulated operating system.

Inspect the generated app entry source and the initial ContentView source. Source membership matters: a visible file must belong to the app target or its synchronized source folder. Keep generated resource catalogs. Replace the generated entry declaration and initial view with the complete example below, using one source file if convenient. Remove the old declarations from that scratch target so there is exactly one @main type and no duplicate root type. The example needs no downloaded package, account data, image asset or custom font.

sections.title: Read the complete app from entry point to screen
sections.html:
The following is a complete iOS 17+ app-target example, not a command-line Swift program. import SwiftUI makes the framework declarations available. @main tells the compiler which type provides the executable entry. The colon in FirstStepsApp: App declares protocol conformance. The app's computed body produces a scene description; some Scene hides its concrete type while preserving it for the compiler. A scene is a system-managed presentation scope. WindowGroup supplies content for windows in that scene family; it is not a promise that every device shows several windows.

import SwiftUI

@main
struct FirstStepsApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            WelcomeView()
        }
    }
}

struct WelcomeView: View {
    var body: some View {
        VStack(spacing: 16) {
            Image(systemName: "hand.wave")
                .font(.largeTitle)
            Text("Hello, Demo Ada")
                .font(.title)
            Text("My first iOS screen")
                .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
        }
        .padding()
    }
}

Inside the trailing closure, WelcomeView() constructs a value describing our root. That value conforms to View, whose computed body returns some View. A VStack places descriptions vertically. The labeled argument spacing: controls gaps in points. Text constructs a text description; the string is synthetic visible content. Each dot call adds a modifier around the previous description. The final padding supplies space around the stack. Nothing here starts a request or writes files during rendering.

The braces after WindowGroup and VStack contain builder expressions rather than an imperative list of addView calls. SwiftUI creates and updates platform rendering from those descriptions. The hand.wave string names a system symbol; it is distinct from a named asset in your bundle. Lesson 072 explains those resources and controls, and lesson 073 examines the modifier chain more closely.

sections.title: Choose a simulator and observe launch
sections.html:
Choose the app scheme in Xcode's toolbar and select an installed iPhone simulator destination with a runtime meeting the deployment target. If no suitable device appears, inspect Xcode's platform/runtime settings and the devices and simulators window; a device definition without its runtime cannot launch an app. Select Product → Build to compile. Select Product → Run to install and launch the scratch product in the chosen simulator. A generic iOS device destination can support a build action but is not a concrete simulator to launch.

This simulator exercise does not require provisioning a physical phone or enrolling in a distribution program. If you encounter a signing complaint, first check whether you accidentally selected a physical or generic device rather than the simulator. Real-device execution and distribution have separate setup and entitlement boundaries; they are not needed to prove this greeting. Avoid changing company signing settings to make the learner target run.

Look for both text lines and the symbol. Stop the app from Xcode, change Demo Ada to Demo Lin, and run again. This confirms that the source belongs to the selected product and that you are observing the new build. A stale simulator app or a second similarly named scheme can otherwise mislead you. Write down scheme, configuration, deployment minimum, destination and observed output; these details make a later failure reproducible.

sections.title: Debug one boundary at a time
sections.html:
If the compiler says it cannot find SwiftUI, confirm this is an Apple-platform target using the intended SDK, rather than a plain cross-platform Swift package. If it reports an extra entry point or duplicate declaration, find the generated types you left in the same target. If a file builds nowhere, check membership before changing imports. If an API is unavailable, compare its documented OS availability with your deployment target; an installed new SDK does not waive the older-runtime contract.

If Build succeeds but Run fails, read the Run report and destination status. An unavailable runtime, failed installation and application crash are different problems. If the screen is blank, verify WindowGroup's root and any conditional branches. Use Xcode's issue navigator for compiler messages and the report navigator for action logs. Do not begin by deleting broad directories or reinstalling every tool. A small greeting has few dependencies, so the first actual error usually identifies the relevant boundary.

The active booking demo has an App entry that constructs ContentView inside WindowGroup. Its Tuist manifest separately declares app, unit-test and UI-test products and an iOS 18.2 deployment minimum. That checkout setting is verified source evidence, not our scratch minimum or a universal requirement. It also has company module dependencies and font registration. Your standalone example intentionally uses system resources so it can teach app setup without reproducing that environment.

sections.title: Make a useful first-app handoff
sections.html:
Before proceeding, explain the source path verbally: the selected scheme builds the app target; its sole entry provides a WindowGroup; the root view describes a VStack; SwiftUI renders its children. Name the difference between the project navigator's files and the target's actual compilation inputs. In Android terms, project organization, task selection and runtime destination also differ, but Xcode's scheme is not a complete replacement for every Gradle product-flavor axis.

Add a third Text for a synthetic build note, then predict where it appears and why. Change the title font separately from the stack spacing. Small isolated changes build confidence that you understand the code instead of only recognizing a template. Keep a notebook of actual Build and Run results, including errors you resolved. A preview can be added in lesson 074; it will speed iteration while leaving launch and lifecycle checks necessary.

The native companion is planned at labs/SwiftUIWorkbench. Its author owns the source filenames and project arrangement. This lesson does not require those files or claim they exist. Keep your greeting as an independently complete scratch example, and later compare its entry and configuration with the companion once available.

quiz.question: Which setting defines the oldest OS your product promises to support?
quiz.explanation: SDK and destination selections do not replace the deployment minimum.

quiz.question: Build succeeds for a generic iOS device. What proves simulator launch?
options: Running the app scheme on a concrete installed simulator and observing it
quiz.explanation: A build compiles a product; Run uses a launchable destination and must be observed separately.

quiz.question: Why remove the generated app entry before adding FirstStepsApp?
options: An app executable needs one @main entry
quiz.explanation: Two entry declarations in the same target conflict; unrelated files need not be public.

exercise.brief: Create a learner-owned iOS 17+ SwiftUI app and produce its first repeatable build-and-run record.
steps: Create the iOS App project and inspect app-target membership and deployment settings.
Replace the generated app/root declarations with the complete source above, keeping one @main.
Build and Run using an installed iPhone simulator; record the actual results.
Add a third Text and change the greeting, then repeat the observation.
Explain a target, scheme, SDK, deployment target and destination without treating them as synonyms.
acceptance: The target contains one executable entry and a complete root view.
The recorded destination meets the deployment minimum.
The learner observes the expected greeting after a fresh Run, or records the unresolved launch error.
The record distinguishes compilation from launch and does not claim device signing or distribution verification.
exercise.solution:
The worked source already provides the smallest useful structure. For your variation, add Text("Build note: synthetic fixture") after the second text inside VStack and replace the first string with Hello, Demo Lin. The new text participates as a third child, so it appears below the previous line with the declared gap. It needs no extra lifecycle callback, storyboard or imperative view insertion.

A good record names the scratch app scheme, Debug configuration, iOS 17 minimum, installed simulator name and runtime, and the observed three-line screen. Record Build's compiler outcome separately from Run's installation and display outcome. If only Build was performed, leave launch pending. The repository comparison should identify its App entry at the verified anchor and note its own manifest minimum and dependencies; it should not copy the company target's settings into the learner app. A correct explanation says that changing a Swift string affects a compiled source input, while choosing a simulator selects where a Run action executes.

lessons.title: Views, controls, assets, and SF Symbols
lessons.summary: Read standard control initializers, distinguish assets from system symbols, and assemble an editable synthetic screen without custom UI infrastructure.
objectives: Read control argument labels and projected bindings.
Distinguish bundled assets from system symbols.
Choose semantic controls and explain input configuration limits.
Implement an explicit action without accidental unrelated state changes.

sections.title: Choose a semantic control before drawing it
sections.html:
On Android you can use a Button or make an arbitrary composable respond to a gesture. SwiftUI offers the same design choice, with different APIs. Start with the control that represents the user's action. Text displays content. TextField edits a String. Toggle edits a Boolean choice. Button performs an action. Picker selects one value from alternatives. These types bring interaction and accessibility behavior that you would have to reconstruct around an image with a tap gesture.

This lesson's complete source belongs to one scratch iOS 17+ app target using Xcode 15 or later. Replace the generated App and ContentView declarations with this source, retaining only one entry point. It uses system resources and synthetic input. A Form organizes controls in platform-styled rows; lesson 077 studies editing and collection management in more detail. The controls here are intentionally ordinary so you can recognize the framework vocabulary before studying a company design system.

The @State declarations make the controls interactive. For now, read them as locally owned in-memory values managed by SwiftUI; lesson 075 develops the lifetime contract. A leading dollar sign projects read/write access for a control. It is not Kotlin string interpolation. Passing a normal String to the text argument of TextField would not express where the user's edits should go.

sections.title: Learn the initializer's labels and closure roles
sections.html:
Swift call sites preserve meaningful argument labels. In TextField("Display name", text: $name), the first parameter has no written external label, while text: names the binding parameter. The first string describes the field; it does not store the field's current content. A user edits name through its binding. Likewise Toggle("Reminder", isOn: $reminder) needs a Boolean binding. These labels help you distinguish two values that might otherwise have the same basic type.

Button's title-and-action initializer accepts a trailing closure. That closure runs for activation, not merely when the screen is described. Statements inside it may assign state. The ternary expression in the final Text chooses a display value from current state; it does not maintain a second summary field. Empty strings and absent values are different concepts, and this first control demo intentionally models only an empty String. Later lessons introduce optional selection.

Stepper's range 1...5 includes both endpoints. Picker's tags are Int values because selection is an Int; mismatched tag types can leave selection behaving unexpectedly. Slider edits a Double in the declared range, and Text formats that value as a percentage instead of manually adding a percent sign. DatePicker edits a Foundation Date value while showing only its date component. Date's stored instant and the calendar/time-zone presentation are different, so this fixture does not claim to implement a scheduling policy.

import SwiftUI

@main
struct ControlsApp: App {
    var body: some Scene { WindowGroup { ControlsScreen() } }
}

struct ControlsScreen: View {
    @State private var name = ""
    @State private var reminder = false
    @State private var count = 1
    @State private var priority = 0
    @State private var progress = 0.5
    @State private var date = Date()

    var body: some View {
        Form {
            Section("Synthetic note") {
                Label("Learning card", systemImage: "book")
                TextField("Display name", text: $name)
                    .textInputAutocapitalization(.words)
                Toggle("Reminder", isOn: $reminder)
                Stepper("Copies: \(count)", value: $count, in: 1...5)
                Picker("Priority", selection: $priority) {
                    Text("Normal").tag(0)
                    Text("High").tag(1)
                }
                Slider(value: $progress, in: 0...1)
                Text(progress, format: .percent.precision(.fractionLength(0)))
                DatePicker("Practice date", selection: $date,
                           displayedComponents: .date)
            }
            Section("Resources and actions") {
                Image(systemName: "star.fill")
                    .foregroundStyle(.orange)
                    .accessibilityHidden(true)
                Button("Fill demo values") {
                    name = "Demo Ada"
                    reminder = true
                }
                .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
                Text(name.isEmpty ? "No name" : name)
            }
        }
    }
}

sections.title: A system symbol is not a bundle asset
sections.html:
Image(systemName: "star.fill") asks for a named SF Symbol supplied by the operating system. Image("DemoBadge") instead looks up a named image resource in the applicable bundle. Android's framework/vector-resource distinction is a useful analogy, but the exact names, bundle lookup and symbol versions belong to Apple. Not every symbol in the installed SF Symbols application is supported by every deployment OS. Confirm the symbol's availability when selecting it; this example uses long-established names.

To practice a bundled image, open the scratch app's asset catalog, create an image set named DemoBadge and add your own synthetic illustration. Ensure the catalog is included in the app target. Then replace the decorative symbol with Image("DemoBadge").resizable().scaledToFit().frame(maxHeight: 80). Resizable permits image scaling; scaledToFit preserves its aspect ratio within the proposed space. Without resizable, a frame does not necessarily resize the underlying bitmap. Do not paste that variation before creating the named asset.

Asset catalogs also support colors and appearance variants. A named color uses Color("DemoAccent") after creating that color resource. Verify light and dark variants rather than hard-coding a dark foreground on a dark background. For a package or framework resource, the appropriate bundle may need to be passed explicitly; a directory name is not itself a runtime bundle identifier. Keep the baseline code independent of custom assets so a missing resource cannot obscure the syntax exercise.

sections.title: Labels, decoration, and input affordances
sections.html:
Label combines a visible title with an icon: Label("Learning card", systemImage: "book"). It often communicates intent better than placing an unlabeled symbol next to unrelated text. A decorative star adds no information beyond surrounding content, so this example hides it from accessibility. A meaningful icon-only action should remain a Button and provide a useful accessibility label. Hiding every image indiscriminately would remove information when the picture itself has meaning.

Input configuration describes how the keyboard or control helps the user; it does not validate a business rule. Word capitalization is reasonable for a synthetic display name, but inappropriate for many identifiers. A number-pad keyboard does not prove that pasted text contains only digits. Disabling a Button can communicate eligibility, but the action should still enforce required invariants when those matter. Lesson 077 introduces trimming at an explicit commit point rather than rewriting text on every keystroke.

System fonts and controls respond to environment and accessibility settings. Prefer font roles such as title and body over assuming all labels fit a fixed pixel box. A button style changes appearance while keeping Button semantics. Here borderedProminent gives the fill action visual emphasis; it does not make that action a save operation. The reminder Boolean is merely synthetic UI state, with no notification request or permission side effect.

sections.title: Find the cause of an apparently broken control
sections.html:
If typing has no visible effect, inspect the binding source and target membership before adding a callback. A constant binding deliberately discards writes; it is suitable for a static display fixture, not this editable demo. If Fill changes name but a different field stays unchanged, trace the actual variable passed to that field. Duplicating two variables with similar names does not synchronize them automatically. If a Picker does not retain a selection, check the selection and tag types and whether the chosen option still exists.

If an image is blank, identify whether the initializer names a bundle asset or a system symbol. For an asset, check exact capitalization, catalog membership and bundle selection. For a symbol, check spelling and OS availability. For distorted artwork, review resizable and the aspect-ratio modifier before adding a second frame. A failed resource lookup and a view with unsuitable size are different boundaries.

The active address form uses framework controls through company wrappers, including its text-field wrapper and explicit keyboard and content-type settings. Those names require company modules and cannot be imported into this tiny scratch app. Read that anchor to recognize how a public control boundary can be decorated with design and analytics policy. Do not infer that every custom wrapper validates all input or that the source was executed during this course audit.

sections.title: Change one control and predict its state
sections.html:
Activate Fill demo values and predict that the text field, Toggle and final Text will update because they read the same sources. Count, priority, progress and date should retain their previous values because the action does not assign them. Resetting unrelated values accidentally is a product bug, even if all controls look correct afterward. Add a Reset button only after writing down which fields it should clear.

Use the simulator to check keyboard entry, the Stepper bounds and both Picker choices. Try a long synthetic display name and a larger text setting; note any clipping rather than declaring the screen universally adaptive. A preview can later provide these fixtures quickly, but actual keyboard and focus behavior requires suitable interactive checks. Save the source and your observed sequence as the evidence for this lesson.

For an interview, explain one initializer from the type of its binding through the resulting UI behavior. A strong answer names the value owner, the activation boundary and the resource lookup. Listing control names alone cannot explain why a form updates. These first distinctions are the building blocks for reusable views and explicit data flow in the next lessons.

quiz.question: What does Image("DemoBadge") require?
options: An SF Symbol with that name
A matching bundled image asset in the correct resource bundle
quiz.explanation: The unlabeled name initializer resolves a resource; systemName selects a system symbol.

quiz.question: A Picker selection is Int. Which tag should its options use?
options: A new UUID each body evaluation
quiz.explanation: Tag type and value must match the selection contract; display text and identity are separate.

quiz.question: Why use Button for the fill action?
options: It supplies activation semantics and control behavior
quiz.explanation: Its action updates synthetic values; persistence and validation remain independent.

exercise.brief: Run the controls demo and add an explicit Reset action plus a bundled-image variation.
steps: Use the complete source as the only app/root entry in an iOS 17+ scratch target.
Predict Fill's effects, then record the actual control updates.
Add Reset with the specified field policy before implementing it.
Create DemoBadge in the scratch asset catalog and try the optional resizable image variation.
Record keyboard, Picker tag, Stepper bounds and missing-resource diagnoses.
acceptance: Fill changes name and reminder through their original sources.
Reset clears name and reminder and returns count to one while preserving the chosen practice date.
The image variation names an actual learner-created asset.
The record separates an asset lookup from a system symbol lookup and does not treat input configuration as validation.
exercise.solution:
Inside the actions Section, add Button("Reset inputs") { name = ""; reminder = false; count = 1 }. Its closure implements the stated policy directly; it deliberately leaves priority, progress and date unchanged. To clear those too, change the written acceptance contract first. The final Text should now display No name because it derives its presentation from the empty source.

The image variation is valid only after the resource exists in the app bundle. Use the resizable, scaledToFit chain from the resources section and hide it from accessibility only if it remains decorative. If the asset is missing, return to the system-symbol baseline while investigating catalog membership; changing observation wrappers would not fix lookup. A worked observation record should mention that the Stepper remains between one and five, Picker tags match Int, and typing edits the same name seen by the summary. No notification is scheduled by the reminder Toggle and no disk record is created. These boundaries should remain explicit in your explanation.

lessons.title: Compose views with stacks and ordered modifiers
lessons.summary: Build small reusable views, read builder syntax, and predict how stack alignment and modifier order affect the result.
objectives: Compose HStack, VStack and ZStack for explicit visual relationships.
Explain generic content and basic ViewBuilder syntax.
Predict padding and background order.
Diagnose overflow through layout relationships rather than random identity changes.

sections.title: A container expresses a relationship between children
sections.html:
Compose's Row, Column and Box give you a familiar starting point. SwiftUI's HStack arranges children horizontally, VStack vertically, and ZStack in overlapping layers. These are conceptual counterparts, not identical measurement algorithms. SwiftUI negotiates proposed sizes and child responses; a stack does not simply assign every descendant a UIKit frame. Learn the common containers before attempting custom layout or reading the advanced Layout implementation in session 031.

This complete example belongs to a scratch iOS 17+ app target, using Xcode 15 or later. Replace the generated entry and root declarations, keeping one App entry. It includes a generic card and all its types; no company helpers or earlier source files are required. The code uses ScrollView so a taller set of examples can remain reachable. A scroll view is not automatically a good substitute for every List or Form; the container's interaction and data needs still guide that choice.

Extract a subview when it has a useful name and responsibility. Here InfoCard owns the common title, padding and background, while the caller supplies its contents. The card does not own the user's draft or load data. A reusable visual boundary and a long-lived state owner are different design decisions, even if both appear as types named View.

sections.title: Some View and a builder do precise work
sections.html:
Content: View declares a generic type constrained to conform to View. The stored content has that chosen type; this is not a list of arbitrary Android View references. () -> Content is a closure with no parameters that produces a description. The initializer's @ViewBuilder annotation lets the caller write several view expressions and conditional branches in the closure. This initializer evaluates the closure once when constructing the card value and stores the result; it does not store an escaping event callback.

var body: some View is a computed property returning an opaque concrete view type. The compiler knows that type even though callers do not spell its deeply nested structure. The body requirement already uses builder behavior, so multiple child expressions inside a container work without an explicit array. You do not use return before every child. Swift builder syntax has specific supported constructs; a general loop mutating an array of views is not the normal repeated-content pattern. Use ForEach for data-driven children, as lesson 077 will show.

import SwiftUI

@main
struct CompositionApp: App {
    var body: some Scene { WindowGroup { CompositionScreen() } }
}

struct InfoCard<Content: View>: View {
    let title: String
    private let content: Content

    init(title: String, @ViewBuilder content: () -> Content) {
        self.title = title
        self.content = content()
    }

    var body: some View {
        VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 12) {
            Text(title).font(.headline)
            content
        }
        .padding(16)
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
        .background(.yellow.opacity(0.15),
                    in: RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 12))
    }
}

struct CompositionScreen: View {
    var body: some View {
        ScrollView {
            VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 20) {
                InfoCard(title: "Synthetic reading plan") {
                    HStack(alignment: .top, spacing: 12) {
                        Image(systemName: "book")
                        VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 4) {
                            Text("Demo chapter")
                            Text("A longer subtitle can wrap onto another line.")
                                .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
                        }
                        Spacer(minLength: 0)
                    }
                }
                ZStack(alignment: .topTrailing) {
                    RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 12)
                        .fill(.blue.opacity(0.15))
                        .frame(height: 100)
                    Text("New").padding(8)
                }
                Text("Padding then background")
                    .padding(12).background(.orange.opacity(0.3))
                Text("Background then padding")
                    .background(.orange.opacity(0.3)).padding(12)
            }
            .padding()
        }
    }
}

Argument labels distinguish title: from the trailing content closure. self.title names the stored property instead of the initializer parameter. The first generic card call causes the compiler to infer Content from its HStack description. There is no need to introduce AnyView merely to avoid seeing the generic type; type erasure is a deliberate boundary choice, not a beginner prerequisite.

sections.title: Spacing, alignment, and flexible space
sections.html:
The outer VStack uses leading alignment and gaps of twenty points. Leading and trailing follow the reading direction, making them preferable to assuming left and right for text-oriented layout. The inner HStack uses top alignment so the symbol aligns with the top of the multiline subtitle group. Its VStack uses a smaller gap to express a closer relationship between title and subtitle. These values describe visual grouping; they should not encode a guessed device width.

Spacer asks for flexible empty space. The zero minimum permits it to shrink when the row is narrow. It is useful for pushing content apart, but multiple spacers and fixed widths can compete and make a row unreadable. A frame with maxWidth: .infinity asks the wrapper to expand to the finite space offered by its parent, not to render an infinitely wide window. Its leading alignment positions the child within that wrapper.

ZStack draws later children over earlier children. In this example the background rectangle supplies a one-hundred-point demonstration area, and New is placed at its top trailing corner. This fixed height is a fixture for a simple badge area, not a universal layout policy for text-heavy cards. An overlay can decorate an existing view without using an independent ZStack as the main layout container; choose it when the decoration should follow the base view's size rather than establish a separate area.

sections.title: Read a chain from the base outward
sections.html:
A modifier returns a new description around the preceding result. Padding followed by background colors the padded extent. Background followed by padding colors the original text extent and then adds uncolored outside space. Predict these two examples before displaying them. The drawing changes because the background attaches to a different wrapper, not because SwiftUI arbitrarily reorders calls. In Compose you also reason about modifier order, while the exact sizing and drawing contract differs.

Frame introduces a sizing wrapper; it does not imperatively assign dimensions to all descendants. Clip controls drawing overflow rather than fixing a broken text-width negotiation. Offset changes drawn position without reserving corresponding neighbor space. Padding participates in layout. Confusing offset with padding often causes overlap that seems inexplicable when looking only at a screenshot. Begin with the declared child and each successive wrapper instead.

Font and foregroundStyle can flow through the view environment to applicable descendants, while individual child modifiers can override inherited choices. Applying a headline to a whole container can affect more text than expected. The InfoCard explicitly sets its header font and leaves its content's choices available to the caller. RoundedRectangle is a shape description used by background; its corner radius changes decoration, not the model's identity or the existence of a touch action.

sections.title: Composition must remain descriptive
sections.html:
Repeated body evaluation is ordinary. Keep it free of requests, file writes and state mutation. A computed subtitle can read current inputs, but a network request started while returning the VStack can repeat unpredictably. Put event work in actions and lifecycle work in defined task scopes. Extracting code to another computed view property does not make a side effect safe; that property still participates in description evaluation.

Conditional branches can change structural identity. If a child owns local state and you replace it with a different branch, the old storage may disappear. Wrapping a view in a new random id to fix layout makes state preservation worse. Choose stable structure where the same feature continues, and deliberate identity replacement where a new feature instance should begin. Lesson 075 gives a concrete editing experiment.

The repository's address demo uses VStack and HStack for its debug panel and action row. Read its padding then background chain at the verified anchor and explain the same wrapper relationship. The advanced flow layout in session 031 handles a different problem: variable-width wrapping with an explicit measurement policy. You do not need that machinery to build this first card, and its source is not evidence that your card was rendered or measured.

sections.title: Reason about content before adding constraints
sections.html:
Try a long subtitle, a narrow window and large Dynamic Type. If the HStack cannot preserve comfortable text width, consider a vertical arrangement rather than reducing the font to force a fit. If the card's background is unexpectedly narrow, identify whether maxWidth applies before the background. If the badge overlaps meaningful content, check whether it should occupy layout space rather than decorate a corner. Each diagnosis should name the responsible wrapper or container.

Separate layout observation from correctness in other domains. A visually pleasing card does not establish keyboard access, VoiceOver labels or persistence. Use text-specific and window-specific fixtures now, then conduct the broader adaptive checks in lesson 082. Record actual observations, including any truncation, and keep the example synthetic. A novice should leave this lesson able to draw the approximate wrapper tree and justify every stack, instead of memorizing an incantation of padding and frame calls.

quiz.question: Which chain colors the space added by padding?

quiz.question: What does @ViewBuilder on the content initializer permit?

quiz.question: A row overlaps after offset. Why?
options: Offset moves drawing without reserving matching layout space

The card chain similarly pads its inner content before expanding the wrapper and attaching its background, so the decoration follows the expanded card extent. This variation is an explicit layout alternative, not an automatic size-class rule. Record the observed width and text size before selecting it for a product. Do not add .id(UUID()) to force a refresh or start work from the content closure; neither addresses content width. A useful worked answer draws Text → padding → background for the first comparison and Text → background → padding for the second, then explains why the card's internal title style does not require rewriting its caller's subtitle. lessons.title: Previews and safe fixture injection
lessons.summary: Create static and editable preview scenarios, qualify macro availability, and treat preview output as one layer of UI evidence.
objectives: Create explicit static and interactive preview fixtures.
Qualify macro toolchain support and content API availability.
Inject fixture dependencies at the preview boundary.
Distinguish preview rendering from build, launch and interaction evidence.

sections.title: Fast iteration needs controlled inputs
sections.html:
Compose previews help you inspect a component without navigating through an entire application. Xcode previews serve a similar workflow, with their own build and execution environment. They compile code and render a chosen description in a development host. That host can evaluate initializers, bodies and tasks, so it is not a harmless static parser. A preview that constructs a production service may trigger real side effects if the service is written that way.

Begin with explicit synthetic inputs. A fixture is known sample data chosen to expose a behavior: an ordinary name, an empty name, a long name, a loading state or a failure state. Fixtures are not copied user records. A preview describes which fixture and environment to use. Keeping those choices in a named scenario makes a visual issue reproducible and lets another engineer understand which case a screenshot represents.

The complete example targets a scratch iOS 17+ app with Xcode 15 or later. Replace the generated App and root types, retaining one executable entry. It uses no company modules, network services or disk store. The same FixtureHost can be launched as the real app root, so preview and app behavior share the editing description while remaining different execution checks.

sections.title: Separate the macro toolchain from the view's OS needs
sections.html:
#Preview is a macro introduced with Xcode 15's Swift toolchain. The hash prefix invokes macro expansion; it is not a runtime control or an ordinary function declared in your app. Named closures supply preview content. Compiler support, preview infrastructure and the availability of APIs inside the content all matter. A view using SwiftUI Observation needs the relevant iOS 17 integration regardless of how its preview is spelled.

Do not state that all SwiftUI #Preview usage universally requires an iOS 17 deployment target. Apple's Xcode 15 release notes describe SwiftUI preview content for older OS versions using an appropriate availability annotation. Behavior also differs for UIKit/AppKit preview overloads and toolchain versions. Our examples choose an iOS 17 minimum to avoid introducing those backward-deployment combinations in a first app. Check the installed compiler's generated diagnostic and official release notes before changing an older product's deployment target solely to satisfy a preview.

The older PreviewProvider pattern remains a useful alternative for toolchains or targets where the chosen macro configuration is unsuitable. Its static previews property returns content. The small alternative below is complete for its view and can be placed in an appropriate SwiftUI app target; it is not a second app entry. It does not make an unavailable API inside that view become available.

import SwiftUI

struct LegacyGreeting: View {
    var body: some View { Text("Synthetic preview").padding() }
}

struct LegacyGreeting_Previews: PreviewProvider {
    static var previews: some View { LegacyGreeting() }
}

This lesson deliberately uses a stateful wrapper rather than declaring local wrapper state with newer preview-only conveniences. You can explore APIs such as Previewable separately with their actual toolchain requirements; they are unnecessary for a reliable iOS 17 fixture.

sections.title: Inject values instead of detecting the host
sections.html:
FixtureCard accepts ordinary values through its synthesized initializer. It can therefore render different scenarios without inspecting process environment variables or assuming that every development launch is a preview. Name and status are inputs, not global state. The CardFixture namespace holds immutable synthetic strings; static means they belong to the type rather than a separate instance. This is a small fixture organization technique, not a dependency container.

import SwiftUI

enum CardFixture {
    static let ordinary = "Demo Ada"
    static let long = "Demo Ada with a deliberately long synthetic display name"
}

struct FixtureCard: View {
    let name: String
    let status: String

    var body: some View {
        VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 12) {
            Text(name.isEmpty ? "No display name" : name).font(.title2)
            Text(status).foregroundStyle(.secondary)
        }
        .padding()
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
        .background(.blue.opacity(0.1),
                    in: RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 12))
    }
}

struct FixtureHost: View {
    @State private var name = CardFixture.ordinary

    var body: some View {
        VStack(spacing: 16) {
            TextField("Demo name", text: $name)
                .textFieldStyle(.roundedBorder)
            FixtureCard(name: name, status: "Fixture only: no request")
        }
        .padding()
    }
}

@main
struct FixturesApp: App {
    var body: some Scene { WindowGroup { FixtureHost() } }
}

#Preview("Editable fixture") {
    FixtureHost()
}

#Preview("Long name, large text") {
    FixtureCard(name: CardFixture.long, status: "Offline fixture")
        .padding()
        .environment(\.dynamicTypeSize, .accessibility2)
}

#Preview("Empty, dark") {
    FixtureCard(name: "", status: "No record selected")
        .padding()
        .preferredColorScheme(.dark)
}

Each preview constructs the complete view it needs. The long-name scenario injects an accessibility Dynamic Type size through the environment. The dark scenario requests a dark appearance. These modifiers make the selected variants explicit. They do not cover every device width, locale or assistive technology. Use Xcode's canvas device controls to inspect further size variants, and label any exported observation with the actual setup.

A preview of FixtureCard does not automatically inherit dependencies installed on the app's WindowGroup, because it instantiates that card directly. Later, if a component reads a required environment model or ModelContext, its preview must install that dependency too. Supply a synthetic model or in-memory container at the preview boundary rather than patching the view to silently use a production singleton when missing.

sections.title: Give interactive fixtures real writable storage
sections.html:
FixtureHost owns name with State and passes its current value to the card. The field receives the projected binding, while the card receives a display-only String. In an interactive preview session, typing should change the card because both depend on the same source. The wrapper gives storage a stable view identity. Declaring a throwaway variable inside a preview closure and pretending it behaves like SwiftUI-managed state is not an equivalent ownership arrangement.

A constant binding is acceptable when deliberately inspecting a frozen control. Writes into it do not update the constant, so it cannot demonstrate a successful editing interaction. For editable child components, create a small host like FixtureHost, or pass a real observable fixture owned at an appropriate boundary. State ownership is still independent of persistence; stopping or recreating the preview can discard this name.

For future service-dependent screens, inject a service implementation whose response is deterministic. A success fixture and an error fixture should not require the public internet or a real account. Avoid loading data from body, and make any preview-associated task use the injected fixture. Merely naming a class MockLoader does not prove that its implementation cannot reach external services. Inspect its behavior before including it in a scenario.

sections.title: An unavailable preview has several possible causes
sections.html:
If the canvas fails, begin with the target's compiler errors. A missing import, duplicate app entry, absent resource and unsupported API can prevent the preview host from building. Check the selected scheme and destination, preview runtime availability, and source membership. A component requiring a framework bundle may need its resources as well as its code. Increasing random delays or clearing broad caches cannot establish which dependency failed.

If the preview displays an empty state unexpectedly, trace the actual input value. If typing does nothing, confirm you are using an interactive/live preview mode and a changing binding. If repeated refreshes start requests, inspect initializers and lifecycle tasks for real service construction. A preview can rerun those paths; its development context is not a lifecycle guard. First reproduce the same view in the scratch app root to distinguish canvas infrastructure from component behavior.

The active booking address view provides normal, error and prefilled previews, constructs explicit models and registers its company fonts. That source shows why resource and dependency setup matter. Your scratch example uses system fonts and plain inputs, so copying the font registration would add an unnecessary company dependency. The verified source anchors support the comparison; reading them does not prove those previews rendered successfully here.

sections.title: Use a scenario matrix with honest limits
sections.html:
Capture ordinary, empty and long-name cases, then compare light/dark appearance and narrow/large-text behavior. For each observation record the scenario name, destination or preview device, text size, and any visible failure. A screenshot proves an observed rendering at that moment. It does not verify app launch, navigation state, accessibility focus, disk restoration or task cancellation. This is why the first-app Run check remains necessary even after previews work.

Keep fixture construction near the boundary and production component logic reusable. If a missing dependency crashes a preview, add the dependency to the fixture host rather than weakening the component's contract silently. The long-name case should remain synthetic and intentionally awkward; visual coverage improves when fixtures challenge assumptions. Lesson 082 turns these experiments into a broader adaptive and accessibility checklist, while this lesson establishes the small repeatable inputs that make that later work practical.

quiz.question: An editable preview TextField receives .constant("Demo"). What happens to writes?
options: They do not update the constant source
quiz.explanation: Use a stateful fixture host when the purpose is editing.

quiz.question: A preview directly constructs a child that needs an environment model. Who supplies it?
options: The preview boundary must install a suitable fixture dependency
Every preview inherits WindowGroup's dependencies automatically
The Swift compiler synthesizes the model
quiz.explanation: Direct component previews have their own hierarchy.

quiz.question: What does a rendered preview establish?
options: All navigation and lifecycle paths passed
That fixture rendered in that preview configuration
quiz.explanation: Build, launch, interaction, assistive technology and persistence need separate evidence.

exercise.brief: Create ordinary, empty, long-name and editable fixtures without production services.
steps: Add the complete app source to a scratch iOS 17+ target.
Open the canvas and inspect all named scenarios, recording actual failures if any.
Interact with FixtureHost and compare its field with a deliberately constant-binding control.
Run the same host as the simulator root.
Record which evidence comes from canvas, compiler and simulator separately.
acceptance: All fixtures use synthetic data and explicit inputs.
The editable case owns a writable source.
The availability note separates Xcode macro support from OS API requirements.

exercise.solution:
The three previews already encode the requested states. The long-name fixture changes text size without altering the stored string, and the empty fixture displays No display name through the card's ternary expression. The editable host should update that same display after field edits. Compare a constant-binding field only as a frozen rendering example; its lack of changing storage is expected.

A worked evidence note lists the canvas scenarios actually rendered, then a separate simulator Run of FixtureHost. If the preview fails to build, record the first diagnostic and verify the view in the app before blaming state. For a future dependency fixture, construct the model in the host and pass it explicitly or install it through environment at that boundary. Do not add a production fallback to make the canvas appear. The older provider is an alternative declaration form, and official release notes determine backward-deployment details; no deployment change or real network access is required by this lesson's baseline.

lessons.title: Local state, bindings, and view identity
lessons.summary: Own one editable source, pass bindings to children, and distinguish stable rendering from deliberate draft replacement.
objectives: Choose one owner for an editable local draft.
Pass a binding without introducing an independent copy.
Distinguish rendering, value reset and identity replacement.
Define record-switch and persistence policies explicitly.

sections.title: Start by naming the source of truth
sections.html:
In Compose, hoisting a value and its onValueChange callback makes the owner visible. SwiftUI commonly packages that read/write access into Binding. The first question is the same: which component owns the value and decides when to discard it? A parent's value and a child's private copy are two sources unless an explicit policy coordinates them. A live summary should usually derive from the owner's source rather than synchronize a copied String through callbacks.

This lesson uses a scratch iOS 17+ app target with Xcode 15 or later, although State and Binding themselves support older SwiftUI systems. Replace the generated app/root declarations with the complete example, keeping one executable entry. The LocalDraft struct contains ordinary stored values. The editor owns one instance in State and exposes only the access its controls need. Nothing saves to disk or sends data externally.

State is SwiftUI-managed storage associated with view identity. The source declaration still has ordinary value syntax, but repeated construction of the View struct is not the same as replacement of that stored value. Keep owned state private so callers do not accidentally treat it like an ordinary initializer input. The view's struct value is a temporary description, while SwiftUI decides which associated state storage belongs to the current hierarchy.

sections.title: A dollar sign projects access, not a copy
sections.html:
@State private var draft = LocalDraft() asks SwiftUI to manage this local source. The private modifier limits ordinary external access to the declaration. The Binding child uses @Binding var name: String, so it receives access to a source defined elsewhere. It does not allocate an independent name store. The parent's $draft.name projects a binding to the nested String through the wrapper's projected access.

import SwiftUI

struct LocalDraft {
    var name = ""
    var reminder = false
}

struct NameEditor: View {
    @Binding var name: String
    var body: some View {
        TextField("Demo display name", text: $name)
            .textFieldStyle(.roundedBorder)
    }
}

struct LocalEditor: View {
    @State private var draft = LocalDraft()
    var body: some View {
        VStack(spacing: 16) {
            NameEditor(name: $draft.name)
            Toggle("Reminder", isOn: $draft.reminder)
            Text(draft.name.isEmpty ? "No name" : draft.name)
            Button("Clear fields") { draft = LocalDraft() }
        }
        .padding()
    }
}

struct StateHost: View {
    @State private var renderCount = 0
    @State private var identity = 0

    var body: some View {
        VStack(spacing: 16) {
            Text("Parent events: \(renderCount)")
            LocalEditor().id(identity)
            Button("Unrelated parent event") { renderCount += 1 }
            Button("Replace editor identity") { identity += 1 }
        }
        .padding()
    }
}

@main
struct StateLessonApp: App {
    var body: some Scene { WindowGroup { StateHost() } }
}

The synthesized NameEditor initializer accepts the binding as name:. Inside the child, name reads the current wrapped String and $name forwards its binding to TextField. Those forms refer to different capabilities: value access versus a read/write handle. A plain let name: String would be enough for a display-only child, but not for this field.

The clear action assigns a fresh LocalDraft value to the existing state location. Because this is a struct, changing its fields follows value semantics rather than creating a shared reference graph. The summary reads the current name directly. Repeated rendering does not require a listener to copy the field into another summary variable. The struct's memberwise/default initialization and property basics were practiced in the language track; here the new element is SwiftUI's storage relationship.

sections.title: Description reconstruction and storage replacement differ
sections.html:
Type a synthetic name, then activate Unrelated parent event. The parent's counter changes, so SwiftUI may reevaluate descriptions. The editor remains at the same structural location with the same explicit identity value; its draft should remain. The constructor expression LocalDraft() in the State declaration supplies the initial value for new storage, not a command to erase existing storage on every reevaluation.

Now activate Replace editor identity. The host increments identity, so .id(identity) describes a different editor identity. SwiftUI can discard the old editor-associated state and create new storage initialized from LocalDraft. This is an intentional teaching experiment. A random UUID created on every body evaluation would repeatedly change identity and could erase edits during routine updates. Stable IDs are correctness inputs, not just animation hints.

The hierarchy itself also contributes identity. Switching between distinct conditional branches or removing a view can end its local state lifetime. State does not promise survival across arbitrary removal, process termination or scene reconstruction. Navigation and container behavior can preserve some views in a flow, but you should choose the actual owner for any draft that must outlive a particular editor. Moving the source to a common parent is often clearer than hoping a transient child stays alive.

sections.title: Initial input is a seed unless you specify another policy
sections.html:
A common editor accepts an initial record, copies its name into State in init, and expects every later parent input to overwrite the local draft. That expectation is wrong when SwiftUI preserves the existing state identity. An initializer can seed storage for a new identity; it does not define a continual synchronization contract. This behavior may correctly protect unsaved edits, or may show an old draft when the parent switches records without replacing identity.

Choose the desired behavior explicitly. The parent can own the draft and provide bindings, a child can reset identity when the selected record changes, or a model can implement a deliberate replace-record operation. A server refresh should not automatically overwrite typing unless the product defines that conflict policy. Do not add two onChange callbacks that copy values back and forth without a precedence rule. They hide ownership and can produce loops or surprising lost edits.

A custom Binding initializer accepts get and set closures, making transformations possible. That can be useful at a real boundary, but trimming or uppercasing every keystroke can move the cursor and confuse input methods. Prefer a computed eligibility value during editing and normalization at an explicit commit point when suitable. A binding is access; it does not promise validation, atomic transactions, persistent storage or thread safety.

sections.title: Ownership and persistence answer separate questions
sections.html:
The draft survives an unrelated parent event because its owner identity remains. Clear fields changes values under that identity. Replace identity ends one editor instance's storage contract and starts another. Restarting the process creates a new in-memory app with no persisted draft. These four events should not be described with the single word reset. A useful design note says which one the product intends.

State is not an Android ViewModel store, SavedStateHandle or database. The analogy to remember helps explain identity-associated storage, but it does not import Android lifecycle or restoration guarantees. AppStorage and SceneStorage serve selected storage needs with distinct limitations, while SwiftData later supplies a real record store. Do not choose persistence because an annotation's name sounds like state ownership.

The active address demo uses State for its model reference and a separately retained coordinator. Its model uses Observation, which lesson 076 will explain. The verified source demonstrates local ownership but does not prove disk restoration. A weak delegate also needs a retaining owner regardless of whether UI reads are observed. Keep the language's value/reference distinction, SwiftUI's storage distinction and disk lifetime distinction separate.

sections.title: Explain a disappearing or disconnected draft
sections.html:
If edits disappear, inspect changing IDs, conditional structure and the placement of the owner. If the field changes but the summary does not, check whether they share the same source. If a constant-binding preview ignores edits, that is the fixture's chosen read/write behavior, not a SwiftUI invalidation failure. If a receiving child creates another State value from its binding, that duplicate store may explain the divergence.

Use the complete host to create a repeatable sequence: type Demo Ada, toggle Reminder, trigger the parent event, clear fields, type again, then replace identity. Predict each result before running it. A notebook of values and identity events is more useful than logging every body evaluation and assuming more evaluations indicate a leak. SwiftUI is allowed to evaluate descriptions frequently; your ownership contract should remain correct.

The next lesson moves from a local value draft to a shared observable reference model. It does not replace the principle of one source. It introduces a separate observation mechanism and explicit reference lifetime, with a legacy alternative for older code. Carry the source-of-truth diagram into that change instead of selecting wrappers from their names alone.

quiz.question: What does @Binding in a child primarily provide?
options: Read/write access to an external source
quiz.explanation: The source is supplied by an owner; Binding does not own independent data storage.

quiz.question: Why can .id(UUID()) in body lose typing?
options: It repeatedly replaces identity and associated state
quiz.explanation: The random value can differ during every reevaluation.

quiz.question: Parent input changes after a child seeds State in init. What must be defined?
options: Whether to preserve, replace or parent-own the draft
quiz.explanation: The initial seed does not automatically synchronize later input.

exercise.brief: Demonstrate the difference between an unrelated update, clearing values and replacing editor identity.
steps: Use the complete host in the scratch app target.
Type Demo Ada and enable Reminder.
Trigger the unrelated event and inspect the retained draft.
Clear fields, type Demo Lin, then replace identity.
Write a record-switch policy for an editor with unsaved changes.
acceptance: The editor and field share one String source through Binding.
An unrelated event preserves edits while identity is stable.
Clear assigns default fields; identity replacement starts fresh editor storage.
The explanation makes no process-death or disk-persistence promise.
exercise.solution:
The expected sequence is Demo Ada/true after the parent event, empty/false after Clear fields, and empty/false after replacing identity following the second edit. The parent event counter stays owned by StateHost, so replacing only LocalEditor does not reset that counter. These are predictions for your observed run, not evidence that a simulator ran here.

For record switching, a parent-owned draft is a straightforward worked design: the parent decides whether to discard unsaved edits, then changes the bound draft after confirmation. A child with its own State instead needs an explicit new-identity or replacement policy. Do not silently overwrite edits whenever a refreshed record arrives. Explain the ownership path as parent state → projected binding → child binding → TextField, and the read-only path as the same current source → summary Text. A constant binding would be a frozen fixture and a local child copy would add a synchronization problem. This solution remains in memory; persistence is an additional contract.

I can pass a binding without introducing an independent copy.

lessons.title: Observation and model ownership, including legacy code
lessons.summary: Share a reference model with read-only and editable children, choose ownership wrappers correctly, and keep isolation and persistence separate.
objectives: Distinguish observation, ownership, isolation and persistence.
Use State, Bindable and plain references for the modern model.
Match legacy StateObject and ObservedObject to ObservableObject models.
Verify derived eligibility and shared reset behavior.

sections.title: A shared model adds reference lifetime to local storage
sections.html:
Your Android feature may share a state holder between an editor and summary. SwiftUI can also share one reference model, while the exact observation and lifetime rules differ from Android ViewModel and StateFlow. A class reference lets both children access the same instance. The owner still decides where that instance lives and when it is replaced. Merely placing a property on a class does not notify the UI of changes.

This complete modern example belongs to a scratch iOS 17+ app target using Xcode 15 or later. Swift's Observation macro was introduced in the Swift 5.9 era, and SwiftUI's integration used here requires iOS 17. Replace the generated app and root declarations with the supplied source, keeping one entry point. Foundation provides whitespace trimming, Observation supplies the macro, and SwiftUI supplies the owner storage, binding adapter and controls.

The lesson is an executable-sized introduction to ideas mentioned in old session 009. It walks from the model declaration to consumers rather than assuming the reader already knows where an iOS model comes from. The synthetic ReadingDraft is in memory; adding a class and observation does not save a record, schedule notifications or retain every delegate connected to it.

sections.title: Observable and MainActor have different jobs
sections.html:
@Observable is a macro annotation on the type. The compiler generates observation support for eligible properties. It is not the State property wrapper and does not itself allocate view-associated storage. final class creates a reference type that cannot be subclassed. Its name and reminder are mutable stored properties, while canContinue is a computed Boolean derived from the current trimmed name. Deriving validity avoids keeping another flag synchronized.

@MainActor declares isolation separately. Calls and mutations of this model must obey the main actor's rules. Observation alone does not prevent data races or make arbitrary background callbacks safe. In this UI-sized example, the owner and consumers are also MainActor-isolated. Long-running CPU work still should not occupy the main actor just because the model is UI-related; create an appropriate worker boundary and return a safe result.

import Foundation
import Observation
import SwiftUI

@MainActor
@Observable
final class ReadingDraft {
    var name = ""
    var reminder = false

    var canContinue: Bool {
        !name.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines).isEmpty
    }

    func reset() {
        name = ""
        reminder = false
    }
}

@MainActor
struct ObservedEditor: View {
    @Bindable var draft: ReadingDraft

    var body: some View {
        Form {
            TextField("Demo name", text: $draft.name)
            Toggle("Reminder", isOn: $draft.reminder)
            DraftSummary(draft: draft)
            Button("Reset") { draft.reset() }
        }
    }
}

@MainActor
struct DraftSummary: View {
    let draft: ReadingDraft
    var body: some View {
        Text(draft.canContinue ? draft.name : "Enter a name")
    }
}

@MainActor
struct ObservedRoot: View {
    @State private var draft = ReadingDraft()
    var body: some View { ObservedEditor(draft: draft) }
}

@main
@MainActor
struct ObservationLessonApp: App {
    var body: some Scene { WindowGroup { ObservedRoot() } }
}

The reset method changes two properties on the same object. Every consumer holding that reference sees the updated values under the observation contract. The reference's identity has not changed. A let reference in DraftSummary prevents reassignment of that property, but it does not make the referenced object's fields immutable. Use API/access-control design when a capability really must be read-only; let alone is not a security boundary.

sections.title: State owns; Bindable exposes bindings; reads observe
sections.html:
ObservedRoot constructs the model in State, providing stable local storage for its reference while that root identity remains. Passing draft to ObservedEditor passes the same instance, not a value snapshot. Bindable enables projected properties such as $draft.name for editable controls. It does not create a second draft or choose disk lifetime. A child that only displays values can receive a plain reference, as DraftSummary does.

SwiftUI tracks observable property accesses that participate in body evaluation. The summary reads canContinue, whose getter reads name, and conditionally reads name for the display. The relevant property mutations can therefore update its description. This is different from subscribing indiscriminately to every field through an arbitrary global notification. Keep body reads and derived getters understandable so dependencies reflect the UI's real needs.

Do not recreate ReadingDraft inside the editor's body and pass that fresh object to every child. That would lose the intended stable source. Avoid side effects in model initialization, because candidate construction can happen during description creation even when SwiftUI retains existing state storage. If the model is supplied by an app-level or feature-level owner, pass that reference in; the receiving view need not pretend to create ownership by copying it into private local state.

sections.title: Read the declared model system before choosing wrappers
sections.html:
The older Combine-based pattern remains important in existing applications. ObservableObject is a protocol, and Published emits changes for its wrapped properties. StateObject is used by a SwiftUI view that creates and maintains such an object's stable instance. ObservedObject is used by a receiving view that subscribes to a supplied ObservableObject. Both can retain references during their use, but ObservedObject does not establish the same stable creator-owned instance across repeated description construction.

The following declarations are a complete alternative root and model for that pattern. They can be used in a scratch SwiftUI app supporting iOS 14+; StateObject arrived in iOS 14. Set the app's WindowGroup to LegacyRoot instead of ObservedRoot if practicing this alternative, and do not add a second app entry. It uses no Observation-only model.

import Combine
import SwiftUI

@MainActor
final class LegacyDraft: ObservableObject {
    @Published var name = ""
}

@MainActor
struct LegacyEditor: View {
    @ObservedObject var draft: LegacyDraft
    var body: some View { TextField("Demo name", text: $draft.name).padding() }
}

@MainActor
struct LegacyRoot: View {
    @StateObject private var draft = LegacyDraft()
    var body: some View { LegacyEditor(draft: draft) }
}

Putting StateObject around ReadingDraft would fail its ObservableObject requirements; putting only State around an unchanged legacy model is not a mechanical observation migration. Read the type's protocols, property annotations, subscribers and owner boundaries. A migration may need to preserve publishers, tests, delegates and older-runtime support. That is a bounded engineering change, not a vocabulary substitution.

sections.title: Observation is neither retention policy nor storage
sections.html:
Ask three questions for each model: what changes notify the UI, who owns its instance, and what survives process termination? Here Observable supplies the first mechanism, root State supplies local reference ownership, and no persistent store supplies the third. A pushed summary may continue to share the root's model if that owner remains; recreating the process constructs a new default draft.

An environment can distribute a model to descendants but does not by itself define a business lifetime. A feature-owned model might be cleared on leaving a flow, while an app-owned model might survive several screens. Account changes and unsaved drafts need product decisions. Sharing a class everywhere can increase accidental lifetime and coupling, so do not create a singleton merely to keep typing from disappearing.

The active address demo locally owns its observable form model and separately retains a coordinator because the model's delegate is weak. The active member-ID demo receives a legacy model with ObservedObject. These source anchors demonstrate coexistence. They do not prove a migration is complete, establish the supplying member-ID owner's lifetime, or imply the form persists data. Follow those boundaries when studying the advanced sessions rather than generalizing from one annotation.

sections.title: Verify shared edits and derived eligibility
sections.html:
Type spaces, then Demo Ada. The eligibility summary should reject the whitespace-only input and accept the meaningful name because it trims for the derived check. The actual name source preserves typed characters; eligibility does not rewrite the field. Toggle the reminder and reset. Reset should clear both values while keeping the same model reference. An unrelated root update should preserve that instance under stable identity.

If the summary remains stale, check whether it received the same object and whether body reads the observable property. If typing resets, inspect owner placement and identity. If a mutation triggers an actor-isolation diagnostic, fix the call boundary instead of removing MainActor without reasoning. If callbacks disappear, inspect weak receiver retention rather than assuming Observable keeps delegates alive.

Record model behavior separately from visual rendering. A unit test can prove canContinue and reset under MainActor without proving focus or layout. Lesson 084 will supply a tested capstone pattern. For now, a strong ownership explanation names model creation, binding access, read dependencies and the absent disk contract; that is more useful than calling every model a ViewModel.

quiz.question: An Observation-only model is locally created by a SwiftUI root. Which wrapper fits this example?
quiz.explanation: StateObject requires ObservableObject; the modern root retains its observable reference in State.

quiz.question: Why does DraftSummary use a plain reference?
options: Body reads participate in observation; it does not need projected bindings
quiz.explanation: Bindable is needed for projected control bindings, not every observable read.

quiz.question: What does @MainActor add beyond @Observable?
quiz.explanation: Observation and synchronization are independent mechanisms.

exercise.brief: Practice one shared observable draft and compare its creator and consumer wrappers with the legacy alternative.
steps: Run the modern complete source in a scratch iOS 17+ target.
Check whitespace-only input, valid input, reminder and reset.
Add an unrelated root state event and explain preserved ownership.
Optionally switch WindowGroup to LegacyRoot with all alternative declarations included.
Annotate each model with its observation, ownership, isolation and persistence contracts.
acceptance: The editor and summary share one modern model reference.
Whitespace eligibility derives from current input.
Wrapper choices match the model's actual protocol or macro system.
The explanation does not infer delegate lifetime or disk persistence from observation.
exercise.solution:
The modern owner stores ReadingDraft in State. The editor needs Bindable for TextField and Toggle projections, while DraftSummary only needs reads. Empty and whitespace-only names produce Enter a name; a valid name produces its current display text. Reset clears fields on the same object. In a unit-test target, equivalent model checks must run under the model's MainActor contract.

The legacy owner instead uses StateObject with a LegacyDraft conforming to ObservableObject, and its consumer uses ObservedObject. Both alternatives are internally consistent; mixing only their wrappers is not. A correct source audit identifies the address demo's creator and retained coordinator, then marks the member-ID consumer's upstream ownership as something to trace rather than guessing it. If you add persistence later, record its save/load and account-boundary rules separately. These steps provide a worked answer and expected behavior, not a claim that either target was launched or migrated here.
