lessons.title: Lists, forms, editing, search, and refresh
lessons.summary: Create and edit stable rows, map filtered deletion safely, and keep refresh scoped and honest about its effect.
objectives: Create stable identities for editable rows.
Separate draft typing from validated add actions.
Map filtered deletion to source IDs and define reorder policy.
Await refresh with cancellation and edit-preservation rules.

sections.title: A scrolling collection needs an identity contract
sections.html:
RecyclerView and Compose LazyColumn teach you to separate row data from the visible row instance. SwiftUI List similarly describes a data-driven platform collection, but its reuse and identity mechanics are framework-specific. Form groups input controls into conventional sections; it is useful for an editor but does not itself validate or save the fields. Choose the container for the interaction, rather than treating List, Form and ScrollView as identical visual wrappers.

The complete source targets a scratch iOS 17+ app with Xcode 15 or later. Replace the generated App and root declarations, keeping one entry. All types are included, and all notes are synthetic. NavigationStack gives rows a place to push their editor, but typed path design is deferred to lesson 079. The store is a local State array, so no records survive process restart.

ReadingNote conforms to Identifiable by providing an immutable UUID. That UUID is created when the note is constructed, not each time body reads it. Title is mutable display data, so it is unsuitable as the identity of an editable note. Two notes may also legitimately have the same title. Stable identity keeps editing, deletion and later selection associated with the record rather than its current position or label.

sections.title: Read ForEach and the editor binding
sections.html:
[ReadingNote] is an array; ForEach(visibleNotes) describes one row for each identifiable element. Its trailing closure receives the current note value. $0 inside filter is shorthand for the first closure argument, and the expression selects matches without changing the underlying store. localizedCaseInsensitiveContains provides a user-facing text comparison; it is not a database query or a stable identifier normalization rule.

import Foundation
import SwiftUI

struct ReadingNote: Identifiable {
    let id: UUID
    var title: String
    var finished = false
    init(id: UUID = UUID(), title: String) {
        self.id = id
        self.title = title
    }
}

struct NoteEditor: View {
    @Binding var note: ReadingNote
    var body: some View {
        Form {
            TextField("Title", text: $note.title)
            Toggle("Finished", isOn: $note.finished)
        }
        .navigationTitle("Edit note")
    }
}

@MainActor
struct NotesScreen: View {
    @State private var notes = [
        ReadingNote(title: "Demo arrays"),
        ReadingNote(title: "Demo bindings")
    ]
    @State private var query = ""
    @State private var newTitle = ""
    @State private var refreshMessage = "Not refreshed"
    @State private var refreshToken: UUID?

    private var visibleNotes: [ReadingNote] {
        notes.filter { query.isEmpty || $0.title.localizedCaseInsensitiveContains(query) }
    }

    private func binding(for snapshot: ReadingNote) -> Binding<ReadingNote> {
        Binding(
            get: { notes.first(where: { $0.id == snapshot.id }) ?? snapshot },
            set: { updated in
                guard let index = notes.firstIndex(where: { $0.id == snapshot.id }) else {
                    return
                }
                notes[index] = updated
            }
        )
    }

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack {
            List {
                Section("Add synthetic note") {
                    TextField("New title", text: $newTitle)
                    Button("Add") { add() }
                        .disabled(newTitle.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines).isEmpty)
                }
                Section("Notes") {
                    ForEach(visibleNotes) { note in
                        NavigationLink {
                            NoteEditor(note: binding(for: note))
                        } label: {
                            Label(note.title.isEmpty ? "Untitled" : note.title,
                                  systemImage: note.finished ? "checkmark.circle" : "circle")
                        }
                    }
                    .onDelete { offsets in
                        let snapshot = visibleNotes
                        let ids = Set(offsets.compactMap { offset in
                            snapshot.indices.contains(offset) ? snapshot[offset].id : nil
                        })
                        notes.removeAll { ids.contains($0.id) }
                    }
                    .onMove { source, destination in
                        guard query.isEmpty else { return }
                        notes.move(fromOffsets: source, toOffset: destination)
                    }
                    if visibleNotes.isEmpty { Text("No matching notes") }
                }
                Section { Text(refreshMessage) }
            }
            .searchable(text: $query, prompt: "Find a title")
            .navigationTitle("Reading notes")
            .toolbar { EditButton().disabled(!query.isEmpty) }
            .refreshable { await refresh() }
        }
    }

    private func add() {
        let title = newTitle.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines)
        guard !title.isEmpty else { return }
        notes.append(ReadingNote(title: title))
        newTitle = ""
    }

    private func refresh() async {
        let token = UUID()
        refreshToken = token
        do {
            try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(300))
            try Task.checkCancellation()
            guard refreshToken == token else { return }
            refreshMessage = "Synthetic refresh completed; edits preserved"
        } catch {
            guard refreshToken == token, !Task.isCancelled else { return }
            refreshMessage = "Synthetic refresh failed"
        }
    }
}

@main
@MainActor
struct NotesLessonApp: App {
    var body: some Scene { WindowGroup { NotesScreen() } }
}

The editor receives Binding to a ReadingNote so its field and Toggle mutate the original source. The binding's getter looks up the stable ID on each read; the setter looks it up on each write. This avoids holding a stale array index after insertion, removal or reordering. Its fallback snapshot is a safety policy for a disappeared row, and its setter discards writes when that row no longer exists. A production design should also tell the user that editing a deleted record is no longer available.

The custom initializer uses a default UUID argument. Swift evaluates that argument for a new construction, so a newly added note receives a new stable identity even if its title repeats. Foundation supplies UUID and trimming. No imported company row type or helper is required by the sample.

sections.title: Separate typing, validation, and commit
sections.html:
New title is a draft String. The Add button derives its disabled state from the trimmed draft, providing immediate feedback without erasing spaces as the user types. The add method checks the same rule at the action boundary, constructs a note and clears the input only after the append. The guard exits before mutation when the input is invalid. This mirrors an Android state holder's explicit event handler rather than assuming a disabled composable is the only validation layer.

Editing uses a Form because the destination contains labeled inputs. That edit is live: every keystroke updates the note through its binding. Navigating back therefore preserves those changes. If the product needs Cancel to discard changes, the editor must own a temporary draft and perform an explicit commit instead; adding a Cancel label to this live-binding editor would not undo mutations. Lesson 080 demonstrates staged modal editing.

The sample permits an empty existing title and displays Untitled as its list label. That is a declared teaching policy, not an accidental inconsistency with Add. A real product could instead require validation before committing edits. Write that rule deliberately and test both creation and editing. Derived UI state helps communicate a rule; it does not decide the domain policy for you.

sections.title: Filtered offsets do not identify source rows
sections.html:
onDelete supplies offsets in the visible ForEach collection. When search hides rows, offset zero may name the second or tenth note in the full array. Removing index zero directly from notes would delete the wrong record. The handler snapshots visibleNotes, maps its offsets to IDs, then removes those IDs from the source. Computing IDs before mutation also avoids shifting indices between deletions. Set collects the chosen identities for membership checks.

Reordering under a filter is a separate policy problem. Should dragging two visible matches change their positions among hidden rows, or change only a filtered view? This beginner example allows reordering only when query is empty. The handler also guards that condition independently of disabling EditButton, because not every invocation necessarily comes through that toolbar affordance. With no filter, visible order equals source order and the standard move operation is meaningful.

Search results are derived state. Keep notes as the authoritative array rather than replacing it with the filtered array. Otherwise clearing search cannot recover hidden records, and editing can affect a copy. Stable IDs let you apply source mutations even as the displayed subset changes. This is the same correctness principle you use for Android list keys, while the SwiftUI callback shapes remain different.

sections.title: Await refresh directly and preserve local edits
sections.html:
The refreshable closure is asynchronous. It awaits refresh directly so the platform's refresh affordance can follow that work's duration. Launching an unstructured Task and immediately returning would detach the operation from that closure's completion. The synthetic refresh waits briefly, checks cancellation and updates a status message; it does not pretend to synchronize a backend or replace edited notes.

The token prevents an obsolete overlapping refresh from committing over a newer one. Both the success path and the error path check freshness, and cancellation is not reported as a user-visible failure. The delay exists to make the refresh observable in a learner UI; it is not a deterministic test synchronization mechanism. For cancellation and stale-result tests, use controlled completion gates as lesson 081 and the capstone explain.

A real refresh that returns records needs a merge policy for unsaved edits, stable IDs, deletion, pagination and account changes. Do not reset notes to the original fixture merely to make a refresh look successful. A refresh indicator finishing proves only that the awaited closure ended; it does not prove the data is newer, persisted or correct. Report actual network and store boundaries separately when adding them.

sections.title: Practice empty, duplicate, and filtered cases
sections.html:
Create two notes with the same title, search for one term, then delete a visible row. Verify by its identity which source record disappeared. Clear search and inspect the remaining notes. Reorder with an empty query, edit a title and check that its ID stays stable. Enter spaces in the Add draft and confirm the action does not append. These small adversarial cases expose mistakes that an ordinary three-row screenshot misses.

The active demo's ContentView uses a List of destinations, providing a verified simple collection anchor. Its company FilterListView uses its own model and publisher contract; it is not the scratch store or proof of editable persistent-row identity. The beginner sample intentionally establishes IDs appropriate to mutable records before the more complex production material. Do not edit those client sources.

If a row jumps or loses editing state, inspect its identity first. If deletion removes a hidden record, inspect the visible-to-source mapping. If refresh erases typing, inspect the merge policy. If an editor updates a different row after reorder, inspect any captured index. A correct worked explanation can name each boundary without claiming that local State is a database.

quiz.question: Search hides the first source note. What does onDelete offset zero name?
options: Always the first source array element
quiz.explanation: Map visible offsets to stable IDs before source mutation.

quiz.question: Why guard reorder when query is nonempty?
options: Filtered-to-source reordering needs an explicit policy
quiz.explanation: The beginner policy permits moves only when displayed and source order match.

quiz.question: Why await refresh directly inside refreshable?
options: The closure's lifetime should include the refresh work
quiz.explanation: Detached tasks can outlive the affordance and need separate ownership.

exercise.brief: Implement CRUD-like in-memory editing and prove filtered deletion targets the right record.
steps: Use the complete source and add two same-title synthetic notes.
Search to hide earlier rows and delete a visible match.
Clear search and identify the removed ID rather than relying only on its title.
Edit a note and reorder with no filter; keep IDs unchanged.
Run synthetic refresh and inspect whether edits persist.
acceptance: Blank trimmed input is rejected at the action boundary.
Duplicate titles have distinct stable IDs.
Filtered deletion maps through visible IDs before mutating notes.
Reordering is explicitly disabled/guarded under search.
Refresh preserves edits and cancellation is not presented as a domain failure.
exercise.solution:
Suppose the source order is A, B, C and search shows only B, C. Deleting visible offset zero should remove B. The handler snapshots that subset and obtains B's UUID, then removes the matching record from the source. A and C remain after clearing search. Directly removing source index zero would remove A and fail the contract.

Editing a title uses the current ID lookup rather than a captured integer position, so moving the row cannot redirect a later write to another record. If a record disappears, this teaching binding ignores writes; a production editor should additionally present a removed-record state. The live-binding editor has no discard-on-back promise. Refresh changes only its synthetic status and awaits its own work, leaving the note array alone. A complete evidence note lists the fixture IDs, search term, removed ID and actual observed ordering. It marks simulator and cancellation checks as pending when they were not run. Disk-backed CRUD begins in lesson 083.
